items.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Research increasingly recognises meaningful human–nature experiences as key drivers of environmental conservation and stewardship. Despite growing interest in the social dimensions of conservation, limited attention has been given to how visitors understand and perceive urban nature conservation and how such perceptions relate to their willingness to participate in conservation actions. This study addresses this gap by examining visitors’ perceptions of urban nature conservation within the City of Cape Town urban reserves, where research on the human dimensions of urban conservation remains limited. Understanding such insights has long-term implications for urban conservation strategies. Method: This study used a combination of in-depth interviews, online qualitative surveys (SurveyMars), focus group discussions, and the Photovoice method over a 10-month period. Adult participants (n = 101) were recruited through convenience and purposive sampling from visitors to the urban nature reserves in the City of Cape Town. Results: Visitors viewed urban conservation not only in terms of biodiversity protection but also through learning opportunities, conservation values, pro-nature behaviours, and social and cultural experiences associated with meaningful interactions with nature. However, these understandings were often constrained by broader challenges related to access and inclusion. Conclusion: Urban conservation requires moving beyond biodiversity protection alone towards more socially inclusive, people-centred approaches that recognise and support the everyday relationships people develop with nature.</jats:p>
title: Visitors’ Perceptions of Urban Conservation: Experiences, Values and Intended Actions

items.abstract: <jats:p>Illegal bushmeat hunting using wire snares remains a major threat to wildlife in African protected ecosystems, yet its spatial and temporal patterns are often difficult to assess because available information is derived from non-random law-enforcement patrols. This study examined patrol-recorded wire snare removals and snare-related wildlife mortality in the Serengeti-Mara Ecosystem from 2018 to 2024. We quantified annual and monthly variation in recorded snares and mortality, modelled annual relative snare occurrence suitability, mapped relative species-specific snare-related mortality suitability for the eight most frequently recorded species, and assessed associated environmental and anthropogenic variables. Kruskal–Wallis tests, Dunn’s post hoc comparisons and Spearman’s rank correlations were used to evaluate temporal variation. Presence-only records were modelled using Maximum Entropy, with continuous predictions retained as relative suitability values from 0 to 1. After data filtering, 87,027 patrol-detected and removed wire snares and 1967 confirmed snare-related wildlife mortalities involving 13 species were retained. Recorded snare removals varied significantly among years and months, with the highest annual total in 2022 and a pronounced monthly peak in August. No monotonic temporal trend was detected in annual snare removals and recorded snare-related wildlife mortality over the seven-year study period. Wildlife mortality also varied significantly among years, months and species, with the highest monthly levels occurring in August and September. Wildebeest accounted for the greatest recorded mortality. Annual MaxEnt models identified recurring areas of relatively high fitted suitability for patrol-detected snare occurrence, particularly in northern and western Serengeti National Park, Grumeti and Ikorongo Game Reserves, the Makundusi grazing lands and Ikona Wildlife Management Area. Species-specific models showed spatial variation in recorded snare-related mortality suitability, while elevation, long-term mean annual precipitation and distance to buildings were among the predictors associated with the fitted patterns. Because standardized information on patrol effort, spatial coverage, and detection was unavailable, these predictions should be interpreted as exploratory patterns of patrol-recorded detections rather than unbiased estimates of the underlying distribution or intensity of illegal hunting. The identified areas and periods may therefore inform field verification and adaptive patrol planning, but should not be used alone to infer snaring intensity or determine patrol allocation.</jats:p>
title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Illegal Bushmeat Hunting in the Serengeti-Mara Ecosystem: Insights from Patrol-Detected Wire Snaring and Wildlife Mortality

items.abstract: <jats:p>Medicinal plants are central to rural health systems and livelihoods in sub-Saharan Africa, yet increasing exploitation threatens their persistence. Pavetta crassipes K. Schum., a shrub widely used in West African savannas, provides remedies for numerous ailments but remains poorly documented in Benin. This study aimed to fill that gap by documenting local knowledge, uses, and conservation perspectives of Pavetta crassipes across all twelve departments of Benin. Data were collected through structured interviews with 582 households and 87 herbal tea sellers, focusing on plant parts used, therapeutic applications, availability, and management strategies. Respondents reported its use in the treatment of about 43 diseases, with leaves being the most frequently cited organ (84.2%). Despite its cultural and medicinal importance, respondents reported declining availability due to bushfires (24%) and leaf marketing (20%), followed by climate change (17%), leaf collection (13%), and tree felling (11%). Conservation strategies mentioned by local communities included planting (26%) and restricting destructive harvesting practices (21%). These findings highlight the dual role of Pavetta crassipes as both a critical health resource and a vulnerable species facing anthropogenic pressures. This study establishes a baseline ethnobotanical database and highlights the need to integrate local practices into conservation planning to secure the future of medicinal plant resources.</jats:p>
title: Ethnobotanical Uses, Perceived Availability and Implications for the Conservation of Pavetta crassipes K. Schum. in Benin

items.abstract: <jats:p>Understanding farmers’ perceptions of ecosystem services (ES) provided by trees in agroecosystems is essential for developing sustainable agricultural landscapes under growing climatic and livelihood pressures. In rice-based agroforestry systems of the Sudano–Sahelian region, trees contribute to productivity, environmental regulation, and rural livelihoods, yet the socioeconomic determinants of farmers’ ecological knowledge remain insufficiently documented. This study examined how socioeconomic attributes shape rice farmers’ perceptions of tree-derived ES in the Niger Valley of northern Benin. Structured interviews were conducted with 401 rice farmers in the communes of Karimama and Malanville to document perceived ES and associated tree functions. Farmers predominantly recognized provisioning and regulating services, including food, shade, soil fertility enhancement, and microclimate regulation, whereas supporting and cultural services such as habitat provision, water purification, and landscape esthetics were less frequently cited. Preferences were largely oriented toward multipurpose tree species that provide immediate livelihood benefits, with preferred key species receiving between 177 and 288 citations. Annual revenue was positively associated with the probability of recognizing at least one ecosystem service, with significant effects for farmers with average annual revenue (β = 0.808, p = 0.005, OR = 2.243) and high annual revenue (β = 0.859, p = 0.037, OR = 2.360). Age and gender were not significant predictors (p > 0.05). However, we found significant associations between formal education and the recognition of selected ecosystem services (Cramér’s V = 0.26, p < 0.001), particularly regulating and supporting services (Cramér’s V = 0.42, p < 0.001).** These findings highlight the role of socioeconomic conditions and differentiated forms of ecological knowledge in shaping farmers’ perceptions of tree-derived ecosystem services in rice-based agroforestry systems in West Africa.</jats:p>
title: Socioeconomic Drivers of Knowledge on Tree-Based Ecosystem Services in Benin Rice Agroforestry Systems, West Africa

items.abstract: <jats:p>Small artificial ponds, known as barraginhas, play a crucial role in providing essential ecosystem services such as soil and water conservation in semi-arid regions. Despite their effectiveness and widespread use in the Brazilian semi-arid region, their effects on biodiversity remain unexplored. Here, we conducted a field experiment to evaluate whether barraginhas constructed along roads to prevent soil erosion influence the diversity of terrestrial insects, specifically ants and beetles. A total of four sampling events were conducted at the beginning and end of both the dry and rainy seasons to assess the effects of the interaction between barraginhas and intra- and interseasonal variation on beetle and ant assemblages. Overall, ant species richness was higher at the end of the rainy season, whereas beetle species richness peaked at the beginning of the rainy season, followed by a secondary peak at the end of rainy season. Importantly, our results showed that barraginhas did not affect beetle richness, whereas ant species richness was significantly higher in barraginha treatment at the end of the rainy season. This seasonal pattern should be interpreted cautiously, as no consistent effect of barraginhas on ant species richness was detected across sampling periods. Ant species composition varied across all sampling months but was not influenced by barraginhas. Similarly, beetle species composition was unaffected by barraginhas and did not differ among the analyzed sampling moths. Given the ecological and economic importance of insects and their global decline across many taxa and functional groups, initiatives to promote conservation and enhance local biodiversity are critical. Finally, we suggest conducting similar studies in different environments and across various taxonomic groups, including plants, other invertebrates, and vertebrates, since barraginhas can also contribute to biodiversity enhancement specially in arid and semi-arid regions.</jats:p>
title: Nature-Based Solutions: Examining the Effects of Small Artificial Ponds on Insect Diversity and Their Implications for the Brazilian Semi-Arid Region

items.abstract: <jats:p>In 2022, Australia became a signatory to the Convention on Biological Diversity’s Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which included commitments to contribute to restoration of 30% of all degraded ecosystems (Target 2) and the achievement of at least 30% protection and conservation of land and seas by 2030 (Target 3). As part of its response towards delivering on Target 3, the Australian Government released its ‘National Roadmap for Protecting and Conserving 30% of Australia’s Land by 2030’ in 2024, which has underpinned subsequent policy and program development. As part of these initiatives, the Australian Government published a technical report in early 2026 prepared by Environment Information Australia to identify priority locations for the protection and conservation of biodiversity, including opportunities to enhance the representativeness of Australia’s protected areas. Here, we review the policy context for these prioritizations and assess how well the spatial prioritization framework, objectives, data, and outputs respond to these policy needs. We outline several fundamental concerns with the approach, including that the prioritization framework was not designed around measurable planning objectives; instead, “components” to be scored are identified, but no targets or outcomes are set against which the maps could be tested; and that it deviates from the science-based approach which has been used to identify priorities for addition to the National Reserve System since the mid-1990s. We also raise concerns about the data used within the spatial prioritization, and the implications for achieving 30 × 30 outcomes in the most effective way possible if the prioritization approach from this technical assessment continues to be applied in its current form. Given that the assessment is informing decisions about where to invest in ecosystem protection, enhancement and restoration, we conclude with some recommendations to help guide a revised version of the technical assessment and associated mapping outputs as soon as possible.</jats:p>
title: Building Australia’s National Reserve System for 30 × 30: A Critique of New Biodiversity Datasets and Prioritization Frameworks, and Suggested Improvements to Achieve Effective Outcomes

items.abstract: <jats:p>Gold mining alters tropical forests, but its association with medicinal tree assemblages remains poorly documented in the Peruvian Amazon. We compared taxonomic diversity, floristic composition, and forest structure between three gold-mining-disturbed plots and their corresponding reference forests in San Juan, Huacamayo-Pacal, and Boca Amigo, Manu Province. Six permanent 1 ha plots contained 1878 non-palm medicinal trees representing 182 species and 46 families. Diversity was assessed using Hill numbers, rarefaction and extrapolation, sample coverage, beta diversity, NMDS, PERMANOVA, and structural attributes. Species richness and effective diversity were consistently lower in disturbed plots. Relative to their paired reference forests, species richness was lower by 52.3%, 18.5%, and 22.5%; q = 1 diversity was lower by 69.3%, 35.7%, and 25.2%, and q = 2 diversity was lower by 77.5%, 59.6%, and 26.6%. Basal area was also lower by 43.0%, 33.2%, and 31.2%, respectively. Floristic differentiation was strongest in San Juan, while multivariate composition differed among the six sampled plots (PERMANOVA: pseudo-F = 4.156, R2 = 0.278). These results show consistent differences in medicinal tree diversity between disturbed and reference plots, although the magnitude of floristic and structural contrasts varied among communities.</jats:p>
title: Medicinal Tree Diversity, Floristic Turnover, and Forest Structure in Gold-Mining-Disturbed and Reference Forests of the Peruvian Amazon
